name: Calendula extract
lead: Calendula extract is a preparation from the flowers of Calendula officinalis (pot marigold), used in topical skincare and traditional wound-care products. People use calendula creams, oils and balms to soothe irritated, dry or sun-exposed skin and to support a calmer, healthier-looking complexion; the plant's oil is widely used in skin products.[7]

Laboratory studies have reported anti-inflammatory properties for flower extracts,[4] and human and animal studies have examined it mainly for wound healing.[1] A 2019 systematic review of calendula extract as a single treatment for wound healing covered 14 studies, 7 animal experiments and 7 clinical trials.[1] A small trial measured the skin's mechanical properties after a calendula cream was applied to the cheeks.[5]

In Europe, the EMA's herbal committee recognises calendula flower preparations for traditional use on minor skin inflammation such as sunburn, minor wounds, and mouth or throat inflammation, on the basis of long-standing use rather than clinical trials.[8]

paras: Calendula extract and calendula oil appear in cosmetics and skin-care products; Wikipedia attributes this to the flowers' saponins, resins and essential oils and notes the oil is widely used in skin products.[7] One study applied a newly formulated calendula cream to cheeks and measured skin elasticity, fatigue and hydration with a cutometer, a device used to assess the effects of cosmetic and anti-ageing products.[5] Calendula also features in herbal soothing products for irritation-prone skin.

Ancient Greek, Roman, Middle Eastern and Indian cultures used the flowers as a medicinal herb and as a dye for fabrics, foods and cosmetics, and leaves were made into poultices for scratches and shallow cuts.[7] The EMA's HMPC monograph lists traditional use for minor skin inflammation such as sunburn, minor wounds, and minor mouth or throat inflammation, for people over 6 years (skin) or over 12 (mouth and throat), and advises consulting a doctor if symptoms last longer than a week.[8] Studies have also examined it in a mouthwash for radiation-induced oral mucositis.[2]

Petals and pollen contain triterpenoid esters and carotenoids such as flavoxanthin and auroxanthin, which give the yellow-orange colour. Flowers also contain flavonol glycosides, oleanane-type triterpene glycosides, saponins and a sesquiterpene glucoside.[7] In laboratory studies, extracts have shown possible antiviral, anti-genotoxic and anti-inflammatory effects, and methanol and ethanol extracts showed antibacterial and antifungal activity.[7]

A rodent study found that oral flower extract at 250 and 500 mg/kg reduced induced paw swelling by roughly 51 and 66 percent in one model, and it also reported effects in a chronic inflammation model.[4] A 1996 paper reported that an aqueous extract of the flowers induced vascularisation in an assay, an observation linked to proposed wound-healing effects.[13] A 2006 in vitro study of a laser-activated extract reported cytotoxic and lymphocyte-activating effects.[3]

The 2019 systematic review reported that, in acute wound healing, treated groups showed faster resolution of the inflammatory phase and increased granulation tissue.[1] In the 40-patient mouthwash trial, patients receiving a 2% calendula extract mouthwash were compared with 20 receiving placebo for radiation-induced oropharyngeal mucositis, with antioxidant capacity also examined.[2] The EMA committee noted that clinical studies in leg ulcers and burns had design problems that prevented firm conclusions.[8]

The EMA monograph states that skin sensitisation has been reported, with unknown frequency, and that the preparations are contraindicated in people hypersensitive to plants of the daisy family (Asteraceae).[8]

Newer work studies calendula as a component of delivery systems: solid lipid nanoparticles,[6] chitosan hydrogels loaded with silver nanoparticles and calendula extract,[14] polyacrylamide hydrogel bandages,[15] an alginate hydrogel with calendula glycolic extract tested on 50 rats over 28 days,[9] and a zinc-oxide nanoparticle cream tested on burns in rats.[10] A 2025 in vitro study reported on calendula extract and mortality of Demodex folliculorum mites, which are associated with some skin conditions.[11] A 2025 paper compared herbal wound-care creams, one containing calendula oil, with a placebo and a commercial cream.[12] These findings come from animal or cell models.

The 2019 systematic review included seven clinical trials of calendula extract for wound healing.[1] In a randomized study of 40 head-and-neck cancer patients, a 2% calendula mouthwash was compared with placebo for radiation-induced oropharyngeal mucositis.[2] A study of a calendula cream on mechanical parameters of human skin has also been published.[5] Trials focused on cosmetic skin appearance, such as acne or ageing, were not found.

card.summary: Marigold flower extract used in soothing skincare; studied for wound healing, with no appearance-specific trials found.
card.note: Research is mainly on wound healing and animal or lab models.

quick.overview:
Calendula extract comes from pot marigold flowers and is used in topical products for soothing skin.
Research has examined wound healing and oral mucositis, plus animal and lab work on inflammation; appearance-specific trials were not found.
quick.mechanism: Laboratory studies report anti-inflammatory activity of flower extracts; the mechanism in human skin is not established.[4]
quick.risks: No significant adverse effects of topical use are described; safety data are limited to the small studies cited.

angle.text: Calendula is used in creams, balms and oils to soothe redness and irritation and to help minor scrapes recover, which is how it contributes to a calmer-looking complexion. Research on its cosmetic effects in healthy skin is limited to a small cream study.
